questions.question: Who is email A written to?

steps: Email A begins 'Hi Amer' and is informal, written to a friend.
solution.summary: Email A is to a friend.

questions.explanation: It uses informal language.

questions.question: Who is email B written to?

steps: Email B begins 'Dear Sir' and is a formal complaint to the company.
solution.summary: Email B is a formal complaint.

questions.explanation: It is signed 'Yours faithfully, Malek Alhayek'.

questions.question: Who wrote email B?

steps: The formal email is signed 'Yours faithfully, Malek Alhayek'.

questions.explanation: He is writing about his family's coach journey.

questions.question: What does 'What a nightmare journey!' in email A mean?

options.A: the journey was a terrible experience

questions.correct_answer_text: the journey was a terrible experience

steps: 'A nightmare journey' means a journey full of problems and stress.

questions.explanation: Email A describes everything that went wrong.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'It didn't arrive on time' in email B?

options.A: the coach failed to arrive on time

questions.correct_answer_text: the coach failed to arrive on time

steps: Email B says 'We were disappointed when the coach failed to arrive on time'.

questions.explanation: 'Failed to' is more formal than 'didn't'.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'more than 30 minutes late'?

steps: Email B says 'it was in excess of 30 minutes late'.

questions.explanation: 'In excess of' is formal for 'more than'.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'The next thing that went wrong was...'?

steps: Email B structures the complaint with 'The second issue was...'.

questions.explanation: It is a formal way of listing problems.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'You know that...'?

steps: Email B uses 'You may remember that last Thursday was a particularly cold morning'.

questions.explanation: 'May' makes it polite and formal.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'To top it all...'?

steps: Email B uses 'Finally, to our utter disbelief...'.

questions.explanation: It introduces the last and worst problem.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'Not an apology from anyone.'?

options.A: at no time were we offered an apology

questions.correct_answer_text: at no time were we offered an apology

steps: Email B says 'at no time were we offered an apology of any kind'.
solution.summary: at no time were we offered an apology

questions.explanation: This uses inversion and the passive for formality.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'Luckily...'?

options.A: we were extremely fortunate in that...

questions.correct_answer_text: we were extremely fortunate in that...

steps: Email B says 'While we were extremely fortunate in that we reached the airport just in time'.

questions.explanation: It is a formal way to say 'luckily'.

questions.question: What is the formal equivalent of 'by the skin of our teeth'?

options.A: just in time to catch our flight

questions.correct_answer_text: just in time to catch our flight

steps: Email B says 'just in time to catch our flight' instead of 'by the skin of our teeth'.
solution.summary: just in time to catch our flight

questions.explanation: 'By the skin of our teeth' is informal.

questions.question: Why do we use the passive voice in a formal email of complaint?

options.A: to be less direct and more formal

questions.correct_answer_text: to be less direct and more formal

source.reference: Writing box: An email of complaint

steps: The Writing box says passives are used 'to be less direct and more formal'.

questions.explanation: Example: 'We were only informed of the timetable change...'

questions.question: Which example uses a clause of concession?

options.A: Although your company had been recommended to us, the service did not meet our expectations.

questions.correct_answer_text: Although your company had been recommended to us, the service did not meet our expectations.

steps: 'Although...' is a clause of concession, used to give balance.

questions.explanation: It concedes a point before complaining.

questions.question: Which adverb is described as an 'initial comment adverb' in the Writing box?

steps: The box lists realistically and ultimately as initial comment adverbs.

questions.explanation: It comments on the whole sentence.

questions.question: Complete: '______, the fault lies with the supplier.'

steps: The example is 'Ultimately, the fault lies with the supplier'.

questions.explanation: It gives the final judgement.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'deeply ______'.

steps: Email B uses 'deeply disappointed'.

questions.explanation: We were deeply disappointed with the service.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'drastically ______'.

steps: Email B says the service 'will be drastically improved'.

questions.explanation: It means greatly improved.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'completely ______'.

steps: Email B says 'what was, in my view, completely inexcusable'.

questions.explanation: It means unforgivable.

questions.question: How late was the coach in email B?

steps: The coach failed to arrive on time and was in excess of 30 minutes late.

questions.explanation: The driver went to a different pick-up point.

questions.question: Why was the coach late according to the driver?

options.A: he had first gone to a completely different pick-up point
options.C: the coach had a flat tyre

questions.correct_answer_text: he had first gone to a completely different pick-up point

steps: Email B says the driver admitted to having gone to a completely different pick-up point.
solution.summary: He went to the wrong place.

questions.explanation: This was the first problem.

questions.question: What was the second issue with the coach?

steps: The coach's heating system was faulty and did not work properly.

questions.explanation: It was a particularly cold morning.

questions.question: What happened on the motorway?

options.A: the coach broke down because of an engine problem
options.B: the coach ran out of petrol

questions.correct_answer_text: the coach broke down because of an engine problem

steps: The coach suffered an engine problem and broke down on the motorway.

questions.explanation: A replacement coach was arranged.

questions.question: What did Malek ask for in his email?

steps: Malek believes they should receive monetary compensation for the inconvenience.

questions.explanation: He also hopes the service will improve.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'gravely ______'.

steps: The collocation is 'gravely mistaken'.

questions.explanation: If you think I won't take this further, you are gravely mistaken.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'wildly ______' (about information).

steps: The collocation is 'wildly inaccurate'.

questions.explanation: The information was wildly inaccurate, causing me to miss my plane.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'fundamentally ______' (about a process).

steps: The collocation is 'fundamentally flawed'.

questions.explanation: The delivery process was fundamentally flawed.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'vastly ______' (about quality).

steps: The collocation is 'vastly overrated'.

questions.explanation: The shoes were vastly overrated; they needed repairs after a month.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'vehemently ______ to'.

steps: The collocation is 'vehemently opposed to'.

questions.explanation: I am vehemently opposed to travelling with your company again.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'wholly ______' (about the way you were treated).

steps: The collocation is 'wholly unjustified'.

questions.explanation: The way I was treated was wholly unjustified.

questions.question: Complete the collocation: 'blindingly ______' (about a problem).

steps: The collocation is 'blindingly obvious'.

questions.explanation: It is blindingly obvious that there is a serious issue.

questions.question: What is the main difference between emails A and B?

options.A: A is informal (to a friend) and B is formal (to the company)
options.C: A is about a flight and B is about a hotel
options.D: A is formal and B is informal

questions.correct_answer_text: A is informal (to a friend) and B is formal (to the company)

steps: Email A uses informal language for a friend, while email B is formal to the company.

questions.explanation: The register changes with the reader.

questions.question: Which informal phrase in email A means 'it started badly'?

options.A: it didn't get off to a great start
options.D: it was in excess of time

questions.correct_answer_text: it didn't get off to a great start

steps: 'Get off to a bad/great start' means to begin badly or well.
solution.summary: didn't get off to a great start = began badly.

questions.explanation: The coach was half an hour late from the start.

questions.question: What does 'down it came! In buckets!' mean in email A?

steps: 'Rain in buckets' or 'bucket down' means to rain very heavily.

questions.explanation: They got soaked while waiting for the coach.

questions.question: What does 'we caught the plane by the skin of our teeth' mean?

options.A: we only just caught it, at the last moment

questions.correct_answer_text: we only just caught it, at the last moment

steps: 'By the skin of our teeth' means by a very small margin, barely.
solution.summary: They only just caught the plane.

questions.explanation: Email B says the same idea formally: 'just in time'.

questions.question: Why does the Writing box say to 'remain polite and be assertive but not aggressive'?

options.A: a firm but polite tone is more effective in a complaint
options.B: you should shout to be heard

questions.correct_answer_text: a firm but polite tone is more effective in a complaint

source.reference: Writing box: An email of complaint

steps: A good complaint is assertive but polite, so the reader takes it seriously.

questions.explanation: It keeps the email effective and professional.

questions.question: Complete: 'I would like to express in the strongest terms, how deeply ______ we were with your company's service.'

steps: Email B says 'how deeply disappointed we were'.

questions.explanation: 'Deeply' collocates with 'disappointed'.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the passive voice?

options.A: We were only informed of the timetable change at the last minute.
options.B: The company informed us at the last minute.
options.C: We received information at the last minute.
options.D: Someone told us at the last minute.

questions.correct_answer_text: We were only informed of the timetable change at the last minute.

steps: 'We were only informed' is passive; the agent is not emphasised.

questions.explanation: It is less direct and more formal.

questions.question: Which phrase from email A is informal?

steps: 'Guess what' is informal and typical of a message to a friend.

questions.explanation: Email B uses formal equivalents like 'in excess of'.

questions.question: What should a good email of complaint include at the end?

options.A: a clear statement of what you want (e.g. compensation)

questions.correct_answer_text: a clear statement of what you want (e.g. compensation)

steps: Malek ends by requesting monetary compensation.

questions.explanation: It makes the complaint effective.
